abstract: Crosslinking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) has the potential to map the human interactome at high resolution and with high fidelity, replacing indirect, error-prone sampling methods such as affinity pulldown MS. However, the sampling depth of XL-MS remains stubbornly low. We present a crosslinking strategy that splits the crosslinking reaction into two sequential and orthogonal coupling events. The method involves pre-stabilizing the spatial proteome with a fixation protocol inspired by immunofluorescence imaging, followed by a stepwise process that begins with extensively labeling surface-accessible lysines in the cell with N-hydroxysuccinimide (NHS)-modified click reagents. We show that a subsequent copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC) reaction of the installed precursors generates crosslinks at levels approaching 30% of the total signal, as demonstrated by a subtractive approach. The method generates no detectable side reactions or obvious distortions of the spatial proteome. Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) are detected at levels approximately 20 times higher than a conventional DSS-based method, outperforming even enrichable crosslinkers.
